🍎 Lesson plan · 🌍 AI in your world · Lesson 14

Lesson plan: How Apps Choose for You

How video, music and shopping apps decide what to show you next, which signals they read, and how to stay in charge of your feed.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • explain what a recommendation system does and name its two big ideas (more of the same, people like you);
  • list signals an app reads, and explain why actions say more than likes;
  • explain how a filter bubble forms, and name at least three ways to widen their own feed.

Warm-up

Open your memory, not your phone: what were the first three things on your video or music app's home page today? Why do you think they were there?

Collect a few answers. Ask whether two students in the class would see the same home page, and why not.

Reading

Students read the lesson “How Apps Choose for You”. Students look for the two big ideas behind recommendations, five signals an app reads, and three ways to take control of a feed.

Activity: Mini-lab “What the app sees”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 14 and switch on one signal at a time, reading the meter and the guess.
  2. They fill in the worksheet's table for each combination.
  3. They switch on “Watched to the end” and “Scrolled away after 2 seconds” together and read what the app says about mixed signals.
  4. In pairs, they decide which single signal they think real apps trust most, and why.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers open “Why your feed looks like that” in the AI Lab. In “The feed bubble”, they run the feed with no surprises, then with 30% surprises, and compare the variety after 40 rounds.

Discussion questions

  • Apps are usually built to keep you watching. Is that the same as showing you what's good for you?
  • Is a filter bubble always bad? When might “more of the same” be useful?
  • Would you like a button that shows why a video was recommended to you? What would you want it to say?
  • Which of your habits (searching, skipping, watching late) do you think shapes your feed most?

Exit ticket

In one sentence, explain how watching a video to the end changes what you are shown next.

Quick check. Why can a feed shrink into a “filter bubble” even if nobody planned it?
Right answer: You can only watch what's shown, and what you watch decides what's shown next

Easier and harder

Easier. Before the mini-lab, act out a feed: one student is “the app” and shows three picture cards, another “watches” one, and the app shows more of that kind next time.

Harder. Students write a short guide for a younger student: “How to get a more varied feed in 5 steps”, using the words signal, recommendation system and filter bubble correctly.
